oneLineAnswer: A prescription antidepressant for adults with major depressive disorder, usually taken in the evening.
whatItIs: Mirtazapine is a prescription antidepressant, which means a medicine used to treat depression. It is sold as Remeron and as many generic tablets, plus a tablet that dissolves on the tongue. Its chemical structure is tetracyclic, meaning it has four joined rings. The label places it in the piperazino-azepine group of compounds. Its formula is C17H19N3 and its molecular weight is 265.35.
whatItDoes: In the United States it is approved to treat major depressive disorder in adults.
That approval rests on four six-week trials in which it beat an inactive pill, called a placebo.
It also beat placebo on the sleep disturbance and anxiety parts of the rating scales.
The label says the way it improves mood is unclear.
It blocks alpha-2 receptors and two serotonin receptors, which may raise noradrenaline and serotonin activity.
Serotonin and noradrenaline are chemical messengers in the brain, and receptors are the docking sites they attach to.
howPeopleUseIt: The label describes one dose a day, taken by mouth, usually in the evening before sleep.
It says the dose should be reduced gradually rather than stopped abruptly.
One form dissolves on the tongue and must be used right after its blister is opened.
Researchers have also tested mirtazapine for insomnia in older adults, which is not its approved use.

commonSideEffects: In six-week trials the most common effects were drowsiness, increased appetite, weight gain, and dizziness.
Drowsiness was reported by 54% of people taking mirtazapine, against 18% on placebo.
Increased appetite was reported by 17%, weight gain by 12%, and dizziness by 7%.
About 16% of people in those trials stopped treatment because of a side effect, against 7% on placebo.
The label calls the drowsiness prominent and says it can impair judgment, thinking, and motor skills.
seriousSigns: A boxed warning says antidepressants raised suicidal thoughts and behaviors in people aged 24 and younger.
The label reports 14 extra young people per 1000 treated under age 18. It reports 5 extra per 1000 aged 18 to 24.
Serotonin syndrome, a dangerous surplus of serotonin signaling, can occur even when mirtazapine is used alone.
A rare blood condition called agranulocytosis can appear as fever, chills, sore throat, or mouth ulcers.
Rare severe skin reactions have been reported, including DRESS, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Other listed warnings include seizures, activation of mania, low blood sodium, and high cholesterol or triglycerides.
QT prolongation, a change in the heart's electrical signal, is listed along with a risk of dangerous heart rhythms.
Antidepressants have caused angle-closure glaucoma, a sudden rise in eye pressure, in people with narrow eye drainage angles.
The label states that clinically significant liver enzyme elevations have occurred with this drug.
whoShouldAvoid: People taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, or MAOI, an older antidepressant class, must not take mirtazapine.
At least 14 days must pass between stopping an MAOI and starting mirtazapine, and the other way around.
People allergic to mirtazapine or to the tablet's inactive ingredients should not take it.
The label says mirtazapine is not approved for children.
Labels advise caution in older adults and in people with liver or kidney disease, seizures, or heart rhythm risk.
People with untreated narrow eye drainage angles face a risk of angle-closure glaucoma.

interactions: MAOIs are contraindicated, including the antibiotic linezolid and injected methylene blue.
They include SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tricyclic antidepressants, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, tryptophan, buspirone, amphetamines, and St John's wort.
Alcohol should be avoided while taking mirtazapine, according to the label.
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, and rifampin speed up the liver enzyme CYP3A4, which clears mirtazapine, so blood levels fall.
Ketoconazole, clarithromycin, and cimetidine slow that enzyme, so mirtazapine levels in the blood rise.
The label says clotting tests should be watched in people who also take the blood thinner warfarin.
pregnancyAndChildren: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies of mirtazapine in pregnant women. The label says to use it in pregnancy only if clearly needed. Animal studies found no evidence of birth defects. However, rat pups died more often in the first days of nursing at high doses. The label says mirtazapine may pass into breast milk and advises caution in nursing women. Mirtazapine is not approved for children. Two placebo-controlled trials in 258 children with depression did not establish that it works. In one child trial, 49% of those taking mirtazapine gained at least 7% of body weight. The rate on placebo was 5.7%.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The exact way mirtazapine improves mood is not known.
The label does not compare mirtazapine with other antidepressants head to head.
The main depression trials lasted six weeks, so longer-term effects are not described in the sources used here.
Rare side effects are counted from reports after marketing, so their true frequency is unknown.
Whether mirtazapine helps people who do not have major depressive disorder is not settled here.

gaps: NCCIH has no mirtazapine page; the URL returned 404, so no NCCIH content is cited.
LiverTox (NIDDK) has a mirtazapine entry, but the NCBI Bookshelf page was blocked by a bot check and the LiverTox host did not respond, so no liver content is cited from it.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded on licence grounds and are not cited.
The liver warning here comes only from the drug label's transaminase section, since LiverTox could not be fetched.
No dose figures appear in this record by design; it reports what US labeling states rather than a personal protocol.
The two label sources are separate publications from different manufacturers and publishers, but both trace to US FDA-approved labeling, so clinical claims rest on one source family.
No head-to-head comparison with other antidepressants could be grounded from the fetched sources.
None of the fetched sources quantify how often the rare serious reactions occur.
summary: Grounds mirtazapine's identity, its approved use in adult depression, common and serious side effects, interactions, and pregnancy and children data in US drug labeling from openFDA and DailyMed, with PubChem and ClinicalTrials.gov as supporting public-domain sources.
